pages.text: Lekettey admired a bright kite at a neighbourhood stall. “Suppose it costs ten cedis,” he told his grandmother, “and I have no money.” “Then let us make a plan,” she said. “First, is a kite a need or a want?” Lekettey thought carefully. “It is a want.”
sentences: Lekettey admired a bright kite at a neighbourhood stall.
“Suppose it costs ten cedis,” he told his grandmother, “and I have no money.” “Then let us make a plan,” she said.
“First, is a kite a need or a want?” Lekettey thought carefully.
pages.alt: Lekettey and his grandmother standing beside a cheerful market stall looking up at colourful diamond kites hanging under the shade roof.

pages.text: Grandmother nodded. “Needs come first, while wants can wait. Suppose I give you two cedis each Saturday when you finish extra jobs at home.” Lekettey gladly agreed to sweep the compound and wash the bowls.
sentences: “Needs come first, while wants can wait.
Suppose I give you two cedis each Saturday when you finish extra jobs at home.” Lekettey gladly agreed to sweep the compound and wash the bowls.
pages.alt: In a sunny Ghanaian courtyard, Lekettey sweeps neatly with a traditional broom while his grandmother watches with a warm, encouraging nod.

pages.text: Together they cleaned an empty tin with a lid, and Grandmother safely made a narrow slot in the top. Each Saturday, Lekettey dropped his two cedis inside. Once, he passed a sweet stall and wanted to spend a coin, yet he asked himself, “Is a sweet worth delaying my kite?” He kept his savings safe.

pages.alt: Inside his tidy room, Lekettey drops shiny coins into a clean slotted tin on a wooden shelf, smiling with quiet determination.

pages.text: After five Saturdays, Lekettey opened the tin at the table with Grandmother and counted his coins in twos: “Two, four, six, eight, ten—ten cedis!” He had reached his goal.
sentences: After five Saturdays, Lekettey opened the tin at the table with Grandmother and counted his coins in twos: “Two, four, six, eight, ten—ten cedis!” He had reached his goal.
pages.alt: At a wooden table beside Grandmother, Lekettey points happily at five neat pairs of coins arranged in a row.

pages.text: Back at the stall, the kite cost ten cedis, just as Lekettey had supposed. He paid with his own saved coins and held the kite proudly. Grandmother smiled. “You worked steadily and you waited patiently,” she said. “That is how savings grow.”

pages.alt: Lekettey handing his coins to the smiling shopkeeper and holding his bright green-and-gold diamond kite while Grandmother beams.

pages.text: Lekettey had learned four helpful steps: set a goal, make a plan, save a little at a time, and wait patiently. As he set up a tin for his next goal, Grandmother added, “A trusted adult or a bank can also keep savings safe—we can ask about that together.”

activities.question: What is the difference between a need and a want?
options: A need is essential for living; a want is nice to have and can wait
They mean the exact same thing
Wants must always come before food and water

activities.question: How many Saturdays did it take Lekettey to save ten cedis at two cedis each Saturday?

activities.prompt: Put Lekettey’s saving journey in order.
items: Make a plan to earn and save.
Save two cedis each Saturday without spending it.
Count to ten cedis and buy the kite.
